subject: Navigation - VOR Operations
learning_objective: State the collision-avoidance concern when operating in the vicinity of a VOR used for navigation.
question_text: When in the vicinity of a VOR which is being used for navigation on VFR flights, it is important to

choices.label: A
choices.text: make 90 degree left and right turns to scan for other traffic.

choices.label: B
choices.text: exercise sustained vigilance to avoid aircraft that may be converging on the VOR from other directions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: pass the VOR on the right side of the radial to allow room for aircraft flying in the opposite direction on the same radial.

explanation: VORs act as natural convergence points for VFR traffic navigating along radials toward the same station, so pilots should maintain sustained vigilance for converging traffic in the vicinity of a VOR.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Systematic 90-degree clearing turns near a VOR are not standard procedure and could create their own traffic conflicts.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: There is no standard procedure to offset to the right side of a radial; the key point is heightened lookout, not lateral offset.

regulation_reference: AIM, VOR navigation and collision avoidance.

subject: Airport and Seaplane Base Operations - Right of Way
learning_objective: Apply the standard right-of-way rule between a converging airplane and helicopter.
question_text: An airplane is converging with a helicopter. Which aircraft has the right-of-way?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The aircraft on the left.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The aircraft on the right.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The faster of the two aircraft.

explanation: Airplanes and helicopters are both power-driven heavier-than-air aircraft with no special category priority between them, so the general converging right-of-way rule applies: the aircraft to the other's right has the right of way.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The aircraft on the right, not the left, has the right of way under the general rule.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Relative speed does not determine right of way for converging traffic.

source_title: CAX - Commercial Pilot Airplane sample questions
copyright_status: U.S. Government work, public domain under 17 U.S.C. 105. Correct answer independently determined by this project — see question 1 note.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Airspace
learning_objective: State minimum VFR flight visibility above 10,000 ft MSL in Class E airspace.
question_text: Your VFR flight will be conducted above 10,000 MSL in Class E airspace. What is the minimum flight visibility?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 3 NM.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 5 SM.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 1 SM.

explanation: At or above 10,000 ft MSL, 14 CFR 91.155 requires 5 statute miles flight visibility for VFR flight.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: 3 NM is not the unit/value used in this rule (the rule uses statute miles).
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: 1 SM is far below the required minimum at this altitude.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Weather Information / Flight Planning
learning_objective: State the general preflight action requirements applicable to a VFR flight.
question_text: You are pilot-in-command of a VFR flight that you think will be within the fuel range of your aircraft. As part of your preflight planning you must

choices.label: A
choices.text: be familiar with all instrument approaches at the destination airport.

choices.label: B
choices.text: list an alternate airport on the flight plan, and confirm adequate takeoff and landing performance at the destination airport.

choices.label: C
choices.text: obtain weather reports, forecasts, and fuel requirements for the flight.

explanation: 14 CFR 91.103 requires every pilot, before beginning a flight, to become familiar with all available information concerning that flight, including weather reports and forecasts and fuel requirements — this general preflight-action duty applies to VFR as well as IFR flights.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Familiarity with instrument approaches is an IFR-specific consideration, not a general VFR preflight requirement.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Listing an alternate airport on a flight plan is an IFR filing requirement, not a general VFR obligation.

copyright_status: U.S. Government work, public domain under 17 U.S.C. 105. Correct answer independently determined by this project — see question 1 note.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Weather (Atmospheric Stability)
learning_objective: State the characteristics of an unstable atmosphere.
question_text: What are the characteristics of an unstable atmosphere?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A cool, dry air mass.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A warm, humid air mass.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Descending air in the northern hemisphere.

explanation: Warm, humid air is characteristically unstable, readily rising and forming cumuliform cloud and showery/convective weather when lifted.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Cool, dry air tends to be more stable, resisting vertical motion.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Descending (subsiding) air is generally associated with stability, not instability.

handbook_reference: FAA-H-8083-25 (Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge), meteorology.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Weather (Airborne Radar)
learning_objective: State the limitation of airborne weather-avoidance radar.
question_text: Which is true regarding the use of airborne weather-avoidance radar for the recognition of certain weather conditions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The radar scope provides no assurance of avoiding instrument weather conditions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The avoidance of hail is assured when flying between and just clear of the most intense echoes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The clear area between intense echoes indicates that visual sighting of storms can be maintained when flying between the echoes.

explanation: Airborne weather radar detects precipitation, not all hazardous conditions (such as turbulence in clear areas between cells or in clouds without significant precipitation); it provides no assurance of avoiding instrument weather conditions generally.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Flying between intense echoes does NOT assure hail avoidance — hail can be flung well outside the most intense radar returns.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: A clear area between echoes on the scope does not guarantee visual conditions or safe passage; radar does not detect all hazards.

source_title: CAX - Commercial Pilot Airplane sample questions
copyright_status: U.S. Government work, public domain under 17 U.S.C. 105. Correct answer independently determined by this project — see question 1 note.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Aircraft Systems (Cabin Heat)
learning_objective: State the reason an exhaust-manifold heating system requires periodic inspection.
question_text: Your aircraft has an exhaust manifold type heating system. The exhaust manifold is periodically inspected to avoid

choices.label: A
choices.text: carbon monoxide poisoning.

choices.label: B
choices.text: overheating in the cockpit.

choices.label: C
choices.text: extremely cold temperatures in the cabin.

explanation: A cracked or corroded exhaust manifold used as a cabin-heat source can leak carbon monoxide into the cabin air supply, so it is periodically inspected specifically to prevent CO poisoning.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: The inspection is not primarily about temperature comfort/overheating; it is a carbon-monoxide safety inspection.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Cold cabin temperatures are not the safety concern driving this inspection.

handbook_reference: FAA-H-8083-25 (Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge), aircraft systems.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Ground Operations (Snow/Slush)
learning_objective: State the recommended procedure to prevent landing gear damage after departure from a snow/slush runway.
question_text: When departing from a runway that is covered with snow or slush, what could a pilot do to prevent damage to the landing gear due to the conditions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Do not retract the landing gear immediately to allow the gear to air-dry.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Immediately retract the landing gear so it can be heated in the gear wells.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fly at a speed above the green arc of the airspeed indicator to remove the snow and slush.

explanation: Delaying gear retraction after a snow/slush departure allows residual moisture to air-dry, reducing the risk of it refreezing inside the wheel wells and jamming the gear.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Immediately retracting wet/slushy gear risks trapping moisture that can freeze in the unheated gear wells of most light aircraft.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Airspeed relative to the ASI's green arc has no bearing on removing slush/snow from the gear.

handbook_reference: FAA-H-8083-25 (Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge), cold weather operations.

copyright_status: U.S. Government work, public domain under 17 U.S.C. 105. Correct answer independently determined by this project — see question 1 note.

subject: Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds - Downwind Landing
learning_objective: State the expected effect of a downwind landing.
question_text: What should be expected when making a downwind landing? The likelihood of

choices.label: A
choices.text: undershooting the intended landing spot and a faster airspeed at touchdown.

choices.label: B
choices.text: overshooting the intended landing spot and a faster groundspeed at touchdown.

choices.label: C
choices.text: undershooting the intended landing spot and a faster groundspeed at touchdown.

explanation: A downwind landing increases groundspeed for a given airspeed, making the aircraft cover more ground during the flare/rollout — leading to a tendency to overshoot the intended landing spot with a faster groundspeed at touchdown.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Downwind landings tend toward overshooting, not undershooting, and airspeed at touchdown (as opposed to groundspeed) is not materially increased by wind direction.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Groundspeed does increase, but the tendency is to overshoot, not undershoot, the landing spot.

source_title: CAX - Commercial Pilot Airplane sample questions
copyright_status: U.S. Government work, public domain under 17 U.S.C. 105. Correct answer independently determined by this project — see question 1 note.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Performance and Limitations (Climb Aerodynamics)
learning_objective: Describe the change in angle of attack and lift when transitioning to a constant-airspeed climb.
question_text: When transitioning from straight-and-level flight to a constant airspeed climb, the angle of attack and lift

choices.label: A
choices.text: are increased and remain at a higher lift-to-weight ratio to maintain the climb.

choices.label: B
choices.text: remain the same and maintain a steady state lift-to-weight ratio during the climb.

choices.label: C
choices.text: are momentarily increased and lift returns to a steady state during the climb.

explanation: To initiate the climb, the pilot momentarily increases angle of attack (and lift) to establish the climb path; once established in a steady, constant-airspeed climb, lift returns to essentially equal weight along the flight path (a steady-state condition), not a permanently elevated lift-to-weight ratio.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Lift does not remain permanently elevated above weight throughout an established constant-airspeed climb; that describes the transient entry only.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Angle of attack and lift DO change momentarily during the transition to establish the climb, rather than remaining constant throughout.

handbook_reference: FAA-H-8083-25 (Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge), aerodynamics of flight.
source_title: CAX - Commercial Pilot Airplane sample questions
copyright_status: U.S. Government work, public domain under 17 U.S.C. 105. Correct answer independently determined by this project — see question 1 note.

subject: Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds - Engine Failure After Takeoff
learning_objective: State the immediate priority action after an engine failure on takeoff in a single-engine airplane.
question_text: If you experience an engine failure in a single-engine aircraft after takeoff, you should

choices.label: A
choices.text: establish the proper glide attitude.

choices.label: B
choices.text: turn into the wind.

choices.label: C
choices.text: adjust the pitch to maintain VY.

explanation: The immediate priority after an engine failure is to establish the proper glide attitude to maintain safe flying airspeed and avoid a stall, before considering a landing area or other actions.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Turning into the wind is not the first priority and can waste altitude/airspeed margin without a specific landing-site rationale immediately after failure.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: VY is a powered best-rate-of-climb speed; it is not the target speed after a power loss, where best-glide speed and pitch attitude for glide are what matter.

source_title: CAX - Commercial Pilot Airplane sample questions
copyright_status: U.S. Government work, public domain under 17 U.S.C. 105. Correct answer independently determined by this project — see question 1 note.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Certification Requirements (Part 119 Exceptions)
learning_objective: Identify operations a commercial pilot may conduct without operating under 14 CFR Part 119.
question_text: You are acting as a commercial pilot, but are not operating under the regulations of 14 CFR part 119. Which of these operations are you authorized to conduct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: On-demand, passenger carrying flights of nine persons or less.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aerial application and aerial photography.

choices.label: C
choices.text: On-demand cargo flights.

explanation: Certain commercial operations, such as aerial application and aerial photography, are conducted under Part 91 without requiring an air carrier/operating certificate under Part 119; on-demand passenger or cargo common-carriage flights generally do require Part 119 certification.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: On-demand passenger-carrying operations generally fall under Part 119's certification requirements.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: On-demand cargo common carriage generally requires Part 119 certification.

source_title: CAX - Commercial Pilot Airplane sample questions
copyright_status: U.S. Government work, public domain under 17 U.S.C. 105. Correct answer independently determined by this project — see question 1 note.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Performance and Limitations (Load Factor)
learning_objective: Interpret a load factor value stated for a level turn.
question_text: While executing a 60 degree level turn, your aircraft is at a load factor of 2.0. What does this mean?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The total load on the aircraft`s structure is two times its weight.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The load factor is over the load limit.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The gust factor is two times the total load limit.

explanation: A load factor of 2.0 means the total load imposed on the aircraft's structure is twice its weight — this is the standard definition of load factor, and 2.0 G is the expected load factor in a coordinated 60-degree bank turn.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: A load factor of 2.0 in a 60-degree turn is the expected/normal value for that bank angle, not automatically over any limit (most normal-category aircraft are certificated to at least 3.8G).
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: 'Gust factor' is a different concept; the question is testing the basic definition of load factor, not gust loading specifically.

handbook_reference: FAA-H-8083-25 (Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge), aerodynamics of flight.
source_title: CAX - Commercial Pilot Airplane sample questions
copyright_status: U.S. Government work, public domain under 17 U.S.C. 105. Correct answer independently determined by this project — see question 1 note.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Performance and Limitations (High-Speed Aerodynamics)
learning_objective: State a possible result of exceeding critical Mach number.
question_text: What could be one result of exceeding critical Mach number?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Propeller stall.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reduction in drag.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Aircraft control difficulties.

explanation: Exceeding critical Mach number can produce shock-induced airflow separation, buffet, and control surface effectiveness changes, resulting in aircraft control difficulties.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Critical Mach number relates to airflow over the airframe/wing, not propeller stall specifically.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Exceeding critical Mach number typically increases (compressibility) drag, not reduces it.

handbook_reference: FAA-H-8083-25 (Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge), high-speed flight.

copyright_status: U.S. Government work, public domain under 17 U.S.C. 105. Correct answer independently determined by this project — see question 1 note.

subject: Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds - LAHSO
learning_objective: State what to expect when LAHSO operations are in effect.
question_text: What should you expect when you are told that LAHSO operations are in effect at your destination airport?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All aircraft must operate on an IFR clearance due to high traffic volume.

choices.label: B
choices.text: ATC may offer a clearance to land and hold short of a specified point on the runway.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Delays due to low IFR conditions and high traffic volume.

explanation: LAHSO (Land and Hold Short Operations) means ATC may offer a clearance for an aircraft to land and hold short of a specified point on the runway, such as an intersecting runway or taxiway.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: LAHSO does not itself mandate IFR operation for all aircraft.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: LAHSO is not specifically tied to low IFR conditions; it is a capacity-enhancing procedure used in various weather conditions.

regulation_reference: AIM, Land and Hold Short Operations (LAHSO).

copyright_status: U.S. Government work, public domain under 17 U.S.C. 105. Correct answer independently determined by this project — see question 1 note.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Aeromedical Factors (Alcohol)
learning_objective: State the blood alcohol concentration threshold for acting as a crewmember.
question_text: You attended a party last night and you consumed several glasses of wine. You are planning to fly your aircraft home and have been careful to make sure 8 hours have passed since your last alcoholic drink. You can make the flight now only if you are not under the influence of alcohol and your blood alcohol level is

choices.label: A
choices.text: below .04%.

choices.label: B
choices.text: below .08%.

explanation: 14 CFR 91.17 prohibits acting as a crewmember with a blood alcohol concentration of 0.04% or greater, in addition to the 8-hour 'bottle to throttle' rule and the general prohibition on being under the influence — the regulatory numeric threshold is 0.04%, not 0.08% or absolute zero.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: 0.08% is a common ground-vehicle DUI threshold in many jurisdictions, not the FAA aviation blood-alcohol limit.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The regulation's specific numeric threshold is 0.04%, not a zero-tolerance 0.0% standard, though flying with any alcohol in the system carries obvious added risk.

source_title: CAX - Commercial Pilot Airplane sample questions
copyright_status: U.S. Government work, public domain under 17 U.S.C. 105. Correct answer independently determined by this project — see question 1 note.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Airworthiness Requirements (ELT)
learning_objective: State the ELT inspection interval and apply it to a specific scenario.
question_text: You are conducting your preflight of an aircraft and notice that the last inspection of the emergency locator transmitter was 11 calendar months ago. You may

choices.label: A
choices.text: depart if you get a special flight permit.

choices.label: B
choices.text: depart because the ELT is within the inspection requirements.

choices.label: C
choices.text: not depart until a new inspection is conducted.

explanation: ELTs must be inspected within the preceding 12 calendar months (14 CFR 91.207(d)); an inspection 11 calendar months ago is still within that requirement, so the aircraft may be dispatched.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: No special flight permit is needed since the inspection is still current.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The inspection is not overdue at 11 calendar months, so there is no requirement to delay departure.

source_title: CAX - Commercial Pilot Airplane sample questions
copyright_status: U.S. Government work, public domain under 17 U.S.C. 105. Correct answer independently determined by this project — see question 1 note.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Weather (METAR Interpretation)
learning_objective: Determine the maximum altitude to remain clear of clouds below a reported ceiling using a METAR and Class E cloud-clearance minima.
question_text: Given the following METAR: KHOB 151250Z 17006KT 4SM BKN025 OVC040 13/11 A2998, what is the maximum altitude to maintain VFR below the ceiling in Class E airspace below 10,000 feet MSL?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 2,000 feet AGL.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 3,500 feet AGL.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 3,900 feet AGL.

explanation: The ceiling is defined by the lowest broken or overcast layer, here BKN025 (2,500 ft AGL). Class E VFR cloud clearance below 10,000 ft MSL requires remaining 500 ft below clouds, so the maximum altitude while staying clear per that minimum is 2,500 - 500 = 2,000 ft AGL.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: 3,500 ft AGL does not correctly apply the 500 ft below-cloud clearance to the 2,500 ft BKN ceiling.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: 3,900 feet AGL does not correspond to a correct application of the cloud clearance requirement to this METAR's ceiling.

regulation_reference: 14 CFR 91.155 (VFR cloud clearance minima, Class E below 10,000 ft MSL); METAR sky-condition interpretation (ceiling = lowest BKN/OVC layer).
calculation_steps: Ceiling = lowest BKN/OVC layer = BKN025 = 2,500 ft AGL. Required clearance below cloud in Class E (below 10,000 ft MSL) = 500 ft. Maximum altitude = 2,500 - 500 = 2,000 ft AGL.
source_title: CAX - Commercial Pilot Airplane sample questions
copyright_status: U.S. Government work, public domain under 17 U.S.C. 105. Correct answer independently determined by this project — see question 1 note.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Airspace (Class B Entry)
learning_objective: State whether a pilot may enter Class B airspace after ATC responds with 'standby.'
question_text: You would like to enter Class B airspace and contact the approach controller. The controller responds to your initial radio call with "N125HF standby." May you enter the Class B airspace?

choices.label: A
choices.text: You must remain outside Class B airspace until controller gives you a specific clearance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: You may continue into the Class B airspace and wait for further instructions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: You may continue into the Class B airspace without a specific clearance, if the aircraft is ADS-B equipped.

explanation: A response of 'standby' is not a clearance into Class B airspace; the pilot must remain clear until ATC issues an explicit clearance to enter.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Entering the airspace while merely 'standing by' would violate the requirement for a specific ATC clearance before entry.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: ADS-B equipage does not substitute for the required specific ATC clearance to enter Class B airspace.

source_title: CAX - Commercial Pilot Airplane sample questions
copyright_status: U.S. Government work, public domain under 17 U.S.C. 105. Correct answer independently determined by this project — see question 1 note.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Weather (Thunderstorm Hazards)
learning_objective: State the hazard of flying under a thunderstorm anvil, even at distance from the cell.
question_text: You are avoiding a thunderstorm that is in your flightpath. You are over 20 miles from the cell however, you are under the anvil of the cell. Is this a hazard?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No, you are at a safe distance from the cell.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes, hail can be discharged from the anvil.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes, this is still in the area of dissipation.

explanation: Hail can be thrown out from a thunderstorm's anvil well beyond the visible core of the cell, so flying under the anvil remains hazardous even at distances of 20 miles or more.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: 20 miles is not automatically a safe distance when under the anvil, given the hail-discharge hazard.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The anvil hazard described here relates to hail discharge, not specifically to the storm's dissipating stage.

copyright_status: U.S. Government work, public domain under 17 U.S.C. 105. Correct answer independently determined by this project — see question 1 note.

subject: Preflight Procedures - Airport Surface Hazards
learning_objective: State where information about airport surface 'hot spots' can be found.
question_text: You are preflight planning in the morning before an afternoon flight. Where would you find information regarding an "Airport surface hot spot?"

choices.label: A
choices.text: Call the Automated Flight Service Station.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In the Chart Supplements U.S.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In the NOTAMs during your preflight briefing.

explanation: Airport surface 'hot spots' — locations with a history of runway incursions or ground-movement complexity — are depicted on airport diagrams published in the Chart Supplements U.S. (formerly the Airport/Facility Directory).

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: An FSS call is a general briefing resource, not specifically where hot spots are published.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: NOTAMs are for time-sensitive changes, not the standard published location for permanent hot-spot depictions.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Aeromedical Factors (Spatial Disorientation)
learning_objective: State the phase of flight most associated with the somatogravic illusion.
question_text: You are most likely to experience somatogravic illusion during

choices.label: A
choices.text: a rapid descent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: deceleration upon landing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: rapid acceleration on takeoff.

explanation: The somatogravic illusion, a false sense of pitching nose-up, is most associated with rapid forward acceleration, such as during takeoff.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: A rapid descent is not the classic trigger for the somatogravic illusion, which is linked to linear (fore-aft) acceleration.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Deceleration (rather than acceleration) tends to produce the opposite false sensation (a nose-down feeling), not the classic somatogravic illusion as typically tested.

handbook_reference: FAA-H-8083-25 (Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge), aeromedical factors.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Airspace (Alert Areas)
learning_objective: State the pilot awareness consideration when transitioning an Alert Area.
question_text: What must a pilot do or be aware of when transitioning an Alert Area?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All pilots must contact the controlling agency to ensure aircraft separation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Non-participating aircraft may transit the area as long as they operate in accordance with their waiver.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Be aware that the area may contain unusual aeronautical activity or high volume of pilot training.

explanation: Alert Areas are depicted to warn pilots of a high volume of unusual aeronautical activity, such as pilot training, so pilots transiting them should simply be aware of and watchful for this activity.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: No mandatory contact with a controlling agency is required for an Alert Area (unlike some other special-use airspace).
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Alert Areas do not require a waiver for non-participating traffic; they are advisory in nature.

regulation_reference: AIM, special use airspace — Alert Areas.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Certification Requirements (Sightseeing Exception)
learning_objective: State the authorization requirements for local, non-stop sightseeing flights conducted for compensation.
question_text: As a commercial pilot, you decide to start a small business flying non-stop tours to look at Christmas lights during the holiday season. What authorizations, if any, are required to conduct Christmas light tours?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No authorizations or approvals are required if you hold the appropriate category and class rating for the aircraft that will be flown.

choices.label: B
choices.text: You must apply for and receive a Letter of Authorization from a Flight Standards District Office.

choices.label: C
choices.text: You must apply to the FAA to receive an exemption to carry passengers at night within a 50 mile radius of your departure airport.

explanation: 14 CFR 119.1(e) exempts certain nonstop sightseeing flights conducted within a limited radius of the departure airport from Part 119's air-carrier/operating-certificate requirements, so a commercial pilot with the appropriate category/class rating may conduct such local sightseeing flights under Part 91 without additional Part 119 authorization.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: No FSDO Letter of Authorization is required for this specific, regulation-defined sightseeing exception.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: No special night-passenger-carrying exemption process applies here; the operation is simply outside Part 119's scope under the sightseeing-flight exception.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Airworthiness Requirements (Airworthiness Directives)
learning_objective: State the appropriate PIC decision when discovering an overdue Airworthiness Directive before flight.
question_text: You are PIC of a flight and determine that the aircraft you planned to fly has an overdue Airworthiness Directive (AD). Which of the following is an appropriate decision?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No maintenance is available so you wait until after the trip to comply with the AD.

choices.label: B
choices.text: You make the flight because you can overfly an AD by 10 hours.

choices.label: C
choices.text: You cancel the flight and have the aircraft scheduled for maintenance.

explanation: An aircraft with an overdue, applicable Airworthiness Directive is not airworthy for flight; the appropriate PIC decision is to cancel the flight and have the AD complied with before further flight (there is no general 'overfly by 10 hours' allowance for ADs, unlike the 100-hour inspection rule).

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Waiting until after the trip to comply is not permitted; an overdue mandatory AD makes the aircraft unairworthy now.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: There is no general regulatory allowance to overfly an overdue AD by 10 hours (that allowance applies to the separate 100-hour inspection requirement, not ADs).

regulation_reference: 14 CFR 39.7 (compliance with Airworthiness Directives required for operation).
source_title: CAX - Commercial Pilot Airplane sample questions

subject: Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds - Wake Turbulence Avoidance
learning_objective: State the recommended vertical positioning to avoid wake-turbulence vortices from a large aircraft.
question_text: Your flight takes you in the path of a large aircraft. In order to avoid the vortices you should fly

choices.label: A
choices.text: at the same altitude as the large aircraft.

choices.label: B
choices.text: below the altitude of the large aircraft.

choices.label: C
choices.text: above the flight path of the large aircraft.

explanation: Wingtip vortices sink below the generating aircraft's flight path, so flying above the large aircraft's flight path is the recommended way to avoid wake turbulence when crossing its path.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Flying at the same altitude puts the aircraft directly in the path of the sinking vortices.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Flying below the large aircraft's flight path is the most hazardous position, directly in the descending vortex wake.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Certification Requirements (High-Performance Endorsement)
learning_objective: State the training/endorsement requirement to act as PIC of a high performance airplane.
question_text: To act as PIC of a high performance airplane, which training or experience would meet the additional requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Logged at least five hours as SIC in a high performance or turbine-powered airplane in the last 12 calendar months.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Received and logged ground and flight training in an airplane with retractable landing gear, flaps, and controllable-pitch propeller.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Received and logged ground and flight training in a high performance airplane and a received a logbook endorsement.

explanation: 14 CFR 61.31(f) requires received and logged ground and flight training in a high-performance airplane (one with more than 200 horsepower) and a logbook endorsement from an authorized instructor before acting as PIC of such an airplane.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: There is no such five-hour SIC allowance satisfying the high-performance endorsement requirement.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: That description (retractable gear, flaps, controllable-pitch prop) describes the complex airplane endorsement (61.31(e)), a related but separate requirement from the high-performance endorsement.

regulation_reference: 14 CFR 61.31(f) (additional training required for operating high-performance airplanes).

subject: Preflight Preparation - Certification Requirements (Recency of Experience)
learning_objective: Apply the category/class-specific nature of passenger-carrying recency-of-experience requirements.
question_text: You have accomplished 25 takeoffs and landings in multi-engine land airplanes in the previous 45 days. For a flight you plan to conduct today, this meets the PIC recency of experience requirements to carry passengers in which airplanes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Multi or single-engine land.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Single-engine land airplane.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Multi-engine land airplane.

explanation: Passenger-carrying recency of experience (14 CFR 61.57) is category/class-specific: takeoffs and landings logged in multi-engine land airplanes only satisfy currency for multi-engine land airplanes, not for single-engine land, even if performed within the same 90-day window.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Multi-engine recency does not carry over to single-engine land currency; each category/class requires its own qualifying takeoffs and landings.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: The recency was established in multi-engine land airplanes, not single-engine land airplanes.

regulation_reference: 14 CFR 61.57(a) (recent flight experience: pilot in command).
source_title: CAX - Commercial Pilot Airplane sample questions
copyright_status: U.S. Government work, public domain under 17 U.S.C. 105. Correct answer independently determined by this project — see question 1 note.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Cross-Country Flight Planning (Pressure Pattern Flying)
learning_objective: Apply pressure-pattern flying to select a favorable-wind route around a high-pressure system in the Northern Hemisphere.
question_text: There is a high pressure system that is located south of your planned route in the Northern Hemisphere on a west to east cross-country flight. To take advantage of favorable winds, you would plan your route

choices.label: A
choices.text: on the north side of the high pressure area.

choices.label: B
choices.text: on the south side of the high pressure area.

choices.label: C
choices.text: through the middle of the high pressure area.

explanation: In the Northern Hemisphere, wind circulates clockwise around a high-pressure area; on the north side of the high, this produces a west-to-east (tailwind) component for an eastbound flight, so routing along the north side takes advantage of favorable winds.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: On the south side of a Northern Hemisphere high, the clockwise circulation produces an east-to-west (headwind) component for an eastbound flight.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Routing through the middle of a high-pressure area generally means light and variable winds, not a consistent favorable tailwind.

handbook_reference: FAA-H-8083-25 (Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge), meteorology.

copyright_status: U.S. Government work, public domain under 17 U.S.C. 105. Correct answer independently determined by this project — see question 1 note.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Weather (TAF Interpretation)
learning_objective: Interpret a multi-period TAF to determine the forecast ceiling and visibility at a specified time.
question_text: In the following METAR/TAF for HOU, what is the ceiling and visibility forecast on the 7th day of the month at 0600Z? KHOU 061734Z 0618/0718 16014G22KT P6SM VCSH BKN018 BKN035 FM070100 17010KT P6SM BKN015 OVC025 FM070500 17008KT 4SM BR SCT008 OVC012 FM071000 18005KT 3SM BR OVC007 FM071500 23008KT 5SM BR VCSH SCT008 OVC015

choices.label: A
choices.text: Visibility 6 miles with a broken ceiling at 15,000 feet MSL.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 4 nautical miles of visibility and an overcast ceiling at 700 feet MSL.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 4 statute miles visibility and an overcast ceiling at 1,200 feet AGL.

explanation: 0600Z on the 7th falls within the FM070500 group (effective from 0500Z until superseded by FM071000 at 1000Z), which forecasts 4SM visibility and OVC012 — an overcast ceiling at 1,200 ft AGL (US TAF cloud heights are AGL).

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: That figure belongs to the initial (0618/0718) period before any FM group takes effect, not the period covering 0600Z, and it misreads the cloud layer as a ceiling in feet MSL rather than the correct AGL convention.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: The visibility unit is statute miles, not nautical miles, in US TAFs, and the ceiling figure/units given here do not match the FM070500 group applicable at 0600Z.

regulation_reference: Standard US TAF format interpretation (FM groups, cloud height AGL convention).
calculation_steps: 0600Z falls between FM070500 (effective 0500Z) and FM071000 (effective 1000Z), so the FM070500 group applies: 17008KT 4SM BR SCT008 OVC012 -> visibility 4SM, ceiling (lowest OVC/BKN) = OVC012 = 1,200 ft AGL.
source_title: CAX - Commercial Pilot Airplane sample questions
copyright_status: U.S. Government work, public domain under 17 U.S.C. 105. Correct answer independently determined by this project — see question 1 note.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Weather (Cold Front Passage)
learning_objective: State the flying conditions typically expected after passage of a fast-moving cold front.
question_text: You have delayed your flight to allow a fast moving cold front to clear your destination airport before your arrival. What type of flying conditions would you expect after the front has passed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A fast moving squall line with high winds and thunderstorms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clear skies with gusty, turbulent winds and cooler temperatures.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Low clouds, reduced visibility and showery, misty conditions.

explanation: After a fast-moving cold front passes, conditions typically clear quickly, with gusty and turbulent winds and a drop in temperature behind the front.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: A squall line, if present, typically occurs ahead of a fast-moving cold front, not after its passage.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Low clouds and misty, showery conditions are more characteristic of a warm front or occlusion than the typically clear conditions following a cold-front passage.

handbook_reference: FAA-H-8083-25 (Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge), meteorology.

subject: Navigation - GPS Considerations
learning_objective: State a limitation of hand-held GPS units for VFR navigation.
question_text: What is a consideration when using a hand-held GPS for VFR navigation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Position accuracy may degrade without notification.

choices.label: B
choices.text: RAIM capability will be maintained for entire flight.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Waypoints will still be accurate even if database is not current.

explanation: Hand-held (non-certified) GPS units generally lack integrity-monitoring (RAIM) and other safeguards of certified installed systems, so position accuracy may degrade without any alert to the pilot.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Hand-held units typically do NOT provide RAIM/integrity monitoring at all, let alone guarantee it throughout the flight.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: An outdated navigation database can contain inaccurate or removed waypoints; currency of the database matters.

subject: Navigation - Dead Reckoning
learning_objective: State the VFR navigation procedure used when ground references are not visible.
question_text: What procedure could a pilot use to navigate under VFR from one point to another when ground references are not visible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dead reckoning.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pilotage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: VFR is not allowed in these circumstances.

explanation: Dead reckoning uses precomputed heading, time, speed, and wind information to navigate without relying on visible ground references, unlike pilotage, which specifically depends on matching ground features to a chart.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Pilotage specifically requires visible ground references to navigate by, which contradicts the scenario.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: VFR flight without visible ground references (e.g., over featureless terrain or water) is not automatically prohibited; dead reckoning is the standard technique used.

handbook_reference: FAA-H-8083-25 (Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge), navigation.

subject: Emergency Operations - Electronic Flight Instrument Systems
learning_objective: State which instrument is affected by an air data computer failure in a glass-cockpit aircraft.
question_text: You are flying an aircraft equipped with an electronic flight display and the air data computer fails. What instrument is affected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ADS-B in capability.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Airspeed indicator.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Attitude indicator.

explanation: The air data computer processes pitot-static inputs (airspeed, altitude, vertical speed); its failure affects displays like the airspeed indicator, while the attitude indicator typically relies on a separate AHRS/inertial reference source.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: ADS-B In is a separate data-link/surveillance function, not dependent on the air data computer for its basic operation.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The attitude indicator in a glass-cockpit EFIS typically derives from the AHRS, not the air data computer, so it is not the instrument most directly affected.

handbook_reference: FAA-H-8083-6 (Advanced Avionics Handbook), electronic flight instrument systems.

subject: Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds - Go-Around Procedure
learning_objective: State the trim-related pitch hazard when applying takeoff power during a go-around.
question_text: When conducting a go-around, the pilot must be aware that

choices.label: A
choices.text: radio communications are key to alerting other aircraft in the pattern that a go-around maneuver is being conducted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: the airplane is trimmed for a power-off condition, and application of takeoff power will cause the nose to rise rapidly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: flaps should be raised as quickly as possible to reduce drag and increase airspeed for a successful go-around.

explanation: Since the airplane is trimmed for a low-power, nose-down landing configuration, applying full/takeoff power abruptly during a go-around produces a strong pitch-up tendency that the pilot must actively counter.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Radio communication may be good practice, but it is not the specific handling hazard being tested — the pitch-trim effect is the safety-critical awareness point.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Raising flaps too quickly during a go-around can cause a sudden loss of lift ('settling') close to the ground; flaps should be retracted incrementally, not as quickly as possible.

subject: Airport and Seaplane Base Operations - Accident/Incident Reporting
learning_objective: Apply NTSB Part 830 reporting requirements to a flight-control-cable failure discovered after an aborted takeoff.
question_text: On a post flight inspection of your aircraft after an aborted takeoff due to an elevator malfunction, you find that the elevator control cable has broken. According to NTSB 830, you

choices.label: A
choices.text: must immediately notify the nearest NTSB office.

choices.label: B
choices.text: should notify the NTSB within 10 days.

choices.label: C
choices.text: must file a NASA report immediately.

explanation: 49 CFR 830.5 lists 'flight control system malfunction or failure' as a reportable incident requiring immediate notification to the nearest NTSB office, which applies to this broken elevator control cable discovered after an aborted takeoff.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: A 10-day filing window applies to the written report following certain reportable accidents/incidents (830.15), not to the initial notification requirement, which is immediate.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: A NASA (ASRS) report is a separate, voluntary safety-reporting program and is not the NTSB 830 notification requirement being tested here.

regulation_reference: 49 CFR 830.5 (immediate notification — reportable incidents, including flight control system malfunction or failure).

copyright_status: U.S. Government work, public domain under 17 U.S.C. 105. Correct answer independently determined by this project — see question 1 note.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Performance and Limitations (Speed Limitations)
learning_objective: State which speed limitation governs structural safety in smooth air.
question_text: Structural damage or failure is more likely to occur in smooth air at speeds above

choices.label: A
choices.text: VNO.

choices.label: B
choices.text: VA.

choices.label: C
choices.text: VNE.

explanation: In smooth air, the structural speed limit is never-exceed speed (VNE); maneuvering speed (VA) specifically protects against structural damage from abrupt control inputs or gust loads, which is a separate (turbulent-air/maneuvering) concern from the smooth-air overspeed limit.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: VNO (maximum structural cruising speed) marks the top of the normal operating range but exceeding it in smooth, calm air is permitted with caution up to VNE; it is not itself the ultimate structural limit.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: VA is the relevant limit for abrupt maneuvers/gust loads, not for straight, smooth-air overspeed, which this question specifically asks about.

handbook_reference: FAA-H-8083-25 (Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge), aerodynamics of flight.

copyright_status: U.S. Government work, public domain under 17 U.S.C. 105. Correct answer independently determined by this project — see question 1 note.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Weather (Density Altitude)
learning_objective: State the effect of increasing temperature on density altitude.
question_text: As air temperature increases, density altitude will

choices.label: A
choices.text: decrease.

choices.label: B
choices.text: increase.

choices.label: C
choices.text: remain the same.

explanation: Warmer air is less dense, so as temperature increases (for a given pressure altitude), density altitude increases.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Density altitude increases, not decreases, with rising temperature.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Density altitude is directly affected by temperature; it does not stay constant as temperature changes.

subject: Preflight Procedures - Taxiway Signage
learning_objective: Interpret a taxiway direction sign to determine the correct turn.
question_text: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-1E, Figure 61.) Ground control has instructed you to taxi Alpha to Foxtrot to the active runway. According to the sign in the figure, which direction would you turn at this intersection to comply with ATC?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No turn is required.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The turn will be made to the right.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The turn will be made to the left.

explanation: The taxiway direction sign shows the aircraft's current position on taxiway A (the black background/current-position segment), with taxiway F indicated by an up-left arrow to the left of it. Complying with the instruction to proceed from A to F therefore requires a left turn.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The sign shows F in a different segment with its own directional arrow, indicating a turn is required, not a straight-ahead continuation.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: F's arrow points up and to the left, not right, indicating a left turn.
